definition: Beguile means to deceive someone by means of charm.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word beguile. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know beguile should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The market vendor beguiled tourists into paying triple for ordinary prints, chatting so warmly that none of them thought to bargain.
Please sits far below beguile on the ladder: pleasing someone wins a smile and nothing more, with no hold taken over anyone.
Charm stops short of beguile: charm draws people to you and may be entirely honest, while beguile turns that same warmth into an instrument of deception.

To enchant is to delight and captivate — an enchanting host, an enchanting view — with no dishonesty implied anywhere. Beguile borrows that same delight and puts it to work as deception: the beguiled victim is being charmed precisely so they will not notice they are being robbed or misled.

Sweet-talk is light, transparent coaxing — everyone can see the game, and the worst it costs is a favor granted with a knowing smile. Beguile is darker: it hides a genuine deception inside real charm, so the victim never sees the game until the damage is done.
drives people away instead of drawing them in
breaks a pleasant spell instead of casting one
Even at cards with his grandchildren, the retired diplomat played with guile.
Beguile means to deceive someone by means of charm.

The double agent beguiled the embassy staff for a decade: he hosted the best dinners in the quarter, told the funniest stories, and left each evening with one more careless remark filed away in his memory.
Beguile names deception that works through delight.

Enchanting and charming someone can be perfectly innocent, and a cheat can rob you without ever being liked — but to beguile is to make the deceiving itself feel like pleasure, so the victim opens the door and smiles.
Beguile is the storyteller's word for deception that feels delightful while it works.
If the flattery is a means to a favor, blandish — also in this unit — is more exact; if you mean the cunning itself, that is guile.
Beguile keeps the spotlight on the victim's enchantment.

Professor Ambrose's medicine show rolled into town with a banjo, a trained crow, and a crate of amber bottles.
He did not argue that the tonic worked; he made the crowd laugh until arguing seemed beside the point.
For two hours he beguiled the square -- flattering the mayor, naming babies, letting the crow tip his hat -- while his assistant quietly moved from wagon to wagon collecting dollars.
Only days later, once the wagons were gone, did buyers compare notes: the bottles held sweetened river water.
The town remembered the evening as delightful right up until it understood what the delight had been for.
